claims.text: The studied material is an additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy containing dual nanoprecipitates.
The nanoprecipitates are coherent and occur within a fine microstructure.
In situ ETEM can monitor oxidation-induced microstructural changes in real time during high-temperature exposure.
APT can map the alloy's elemental distribution at near-atomic resolution after oxidation intervals.
Combining ETEM and APT will reveal dynamic elemental redistribution within the dual nanoprecipitates during oxidation.
Elemental redistribution within the nanoprecipitates will correlate with changes in oxide-scale formation.
The proposed oxidation conditions are representative of gas-turbine or aerospace operating environments.
The dual nanoprecipitates act as sites for elemental segregation and redistribution during oxidation.
Redistribution at the nanoprecipitates mediates the evolution of a protective oxide scale.
High-temperature oxidation can selectively remove an oxide-forming element from an HEA and deplete that element in the underlying alloy.
Oxidation selectively drives specific elements out of the nanoprecipitates in Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
Selective elemental migration produces compositional gradients and alters both the nanoprecipitates and the developing oxide layer.
Elemental redistribution and the resulting oxide composition affect high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Oxidation will cause observable depletion of oxidation-sensitive elements and enrichment of other elements in the nanoprecipitates.
The nanoprecipitate composition changes will correlate with oxide-scale formation and evolution.
Integrated ETEM and APT will provide mechanistic insights that conventional ex situ methods do not capture.
Conventional ex situ XRD and post-mortem TEM lack the combined nanoscale elemental resolution and dynamic observation needed to fully capture redistribution during oxidation.
The integrated method is effective only when oxidation kinetics are slow enough for real-time imaging and elemental mapping.
Extremely rapid oxidation or interface reactions may exceed the temporal resolution of ETEM or APT and obscure transient phenomena.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes in situ high-resolution APT integrated with ETEM and predicts real-time compositional changes, whereas the intervention and falsification experiment specify ETEM during oxidation followed by subsequent or interval-based APT. The latter is not simultaneous real-time APT measurement of the same oxidation event.
